title: Ai game dev takes endless debugging
author: Chonki_Chonga
selftext:
I see a lot of hate against ai games and people saying its just one prompt and its finnished. But tbh you have to rework an insane amout of time because ai obviously has no idea what makes a game fun.

For sure its less compared to not using ai, but its still a lot of work and i feel like people who just see ai gamedev on tiktok and so on cant understand it

comments.author: Heavy-Revolution-784
comments.body: skill issue. setup your agents to run e2e tests, unit tests, linting tests, playtests, ect. most bugs should get caught in CI. You can just tell your agent to set git hooks to run your tests suites before it can create a commit or push to remote

replies.author: operatingcan
replies.body: OP literally mentions code bugs 0 times

replies.author: HaphazardlyOrganized
replies.body:
All the tests in the world won't make a game fun, you have to play it and get other people to play it.

Plus with how easy it is to launch a game the floor for quality needs to be way higher, and that doesn't mean graphics, it means things like cross compatibility, net code, settings menus, your tutorial, telemetry systems, ect.

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body:
You dont play your games, do you?

Also, your testing workflow sucks, but fixing it doesn't solve the real problem.

comments.author: Valdaraak
comments.body:
>ai obviously has no idea what makes a game fun.

Because that's *your* job, not the AI's. You should be giving the AI long, detailed design documents for all the mechanics, features, characters, story, and so forth that your game will have. AI's job is to help build your vision, not design it entirely. There's only a bunch of rework and refactoring if you didn't have a plan for it to work off of.

replies.author: ipreuss
replies.body: Apparently you have never heard of iterative development…

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body: A design document doesn't take away the need for iterative testing and development. Because you CANNOT know what a game feels like before you have played it. And the moment you play it, all your plans need to adapt.

replies.author: Upbeat-Mail7201
replies.body: A Game Design Document is no matter how well planned always a fluid and living document, it must change during development. Software Development in general, but game development in specific is the most iterative process out there 😅 you cannot and will never make the game 100% like planned beforehand, and that's okay, necessary and unavoidable

comments.author: Signal_Week_4719
comments.body: 80% is playtesting, finding bugs fix em, something doesnt look right fix, balance is not good fix it, add better visuals/sound effects. Its never ending.

comments.author: WhosLive
comments.body: A lot of people hit this wall, because AI can get a working build fast but it can't tell you whether the game is fun. What usually helps is shortening the loop between a change and someone actually playing it. Worth trying a short written goal for each build (what should the player feel in the first two minutes) and then testing against that instead of just fixing whatever looks off. Getting a few real people to play early tends to cut more rework than any amount of extra prompting, since they find the boring parts you've stopped noticing.

replies.author: BinniesPurp
replies.body:
Aha yea I learnt that fairly recently after jumping into this vibe coding shit, 

I been working for indie/AA studios since 10-15 years ago but skipped a good chunk of the start of AI because I CBF, 

After enough people telling me "you turn 6 months of work into 1 hour" and "it can literally just like make Diablo or Minecraft infront of you in seconds" I checked it out and it's so surface level 

It can write individual scripts and attempt to follow the general framework to tie them together but the idea of it self making large scale indie PC games is still absurd 

The examples people give you to provide evidence are basically flappy bird clones or idle games, so so many idle games

replies.author: Spoonman915
replies.body:
Ya. I've been working on a blender add-on to generate crowds and armies. No way I could've done it before. I have zero coding experience. Also vibe-coding a production management tool. 

But I'm going through one feature at a time. Screen shotting, sketch where I want buttons, dividers,  etc. Testing things as I work on a project. When I first gave chatGPT the description and the first prompt, I think it tried to one shot it, or something ended up just freezing my computer by opening 4 copies of blender.

replies.author: BinniesPurp
replies.body:
I gotta ask why you'd make the whole army in blender, wouldn't that usually get pulled over to your engine 

Or else you're copping an fbx with a million polygons that can't be culled

replies.author: Spoonman915
replies.body:
I'm actually developing an animated series. Not a game. I'm here to see what other people are doing with their geometry and graphics.

My current workflow is GPT generating concept art, computer use to generate in tripo, GLB export, and I have GPT handle rigging and weights in Blender. I go back in a make minor adjustments if needed. Currently working through how to take that geo into the crowd generator and populates a battlefield.

I'm working on a shot set at The Battle of Mohacs from 1526. Ottomans v Hungarians. I need about 80,000 Ottoman troops.  My approach is to gen 10-20 different soldiers for each soldier type, cavalry, Jannisaries, infantry, etc. The soldier is split up into helm, head, torso, legs, hands, and boots.

The parts are randomized by the rig and can be set by a desired percentage.That way I have good variety and very minimal repetition, with decent control. Add a few material variations, and almost no repetition at all.

I was able to do it with a static rectangular array with the parts attached to geometry, so now I'm trying to figure out how to do the offsets and variations in grouping, animation, etc. that one might see in that situation.

comments.author: DancinFool82
comments.body: Yeah it's not talked enough about how dumb the decisions the AI make are. At surface level it looks cool but it requires a tremendous amount of effort to actually get anything usable. If used as a tool though I find it incredibly speeds up my development. It's just not the fix-all people claim it is.

comments.author: Ijatsu
comments.body:
Who would have thought that not being a software engineer and architect and delegating everything to AI even their own prompt would end up in full of bug slop?

Prompting agents is exactly like programming but in a natural language. If you suck at programming you'll suck at prompting agents.

And that's even before artistic direction and gameplay design come up.

comments.author: Silent_Wave3137
comments.body: Skill issue. My games are mostly bug free and fairly complex. Create a harness and have an agent whose job it is to break your game. Fable reviews my code weekly and finds several bugs and spawns agents to fix them. It’s pretty rare for players to report bugs and be got a few hundred players at any given time.

comments.body: I think a lot of the problem comes from idiots trying to act like AI can one shot everything and then demoing their projects in an extremely disingenuous way so the average person comes to the conclusion that none of us actually care about gaming and are just trying to make a quick buck using tools they believe are built off the back of other peoples work(through model training)

comments.author: EC36339
comments.body:
That's also what distinguishes actually playable games from slop. Anything that hasn't been playtested can't possibly be fun to play.

You need hands and a mouse and keyboard to know what a game feels like. AI doesn't have thay kind of feedback loop.

comments.author: QuadWingedCrane
comments.body: This is literally what separates a dev from a clanker

comments.author: VG_Crimson
comments.body:
There is something to be said about using it to create systems which are designed by you from an architectural level, and not the "Make a parry System" kind of systems but the kind where you dictate to it what classes/scripts can interact with each other, how they connect, and how your compiled code is organized such that certain types of referencing across code is forbidden to promote design language that is self correcting. Doing all of that takes a long time of setup and speeding that up can help you focus more time on the actual game designs and intricacies of making a game fun and well thought out.

This hands-on type of AI game development is not something you can just convey to the layman masses and them have a nuanced understanding. Only people who know how to program video games without AI might be able to understand your perspective, so it's easier to just see AI as whole-ly one enemy and stolen valor. Especially when the technology already has shown to threaten livelihoods, or in a more relevant topic is responsible for a crap ton of "shitty games AI games" intended to make quick money by grifters who have an interest in video games. Death by association.

comments.author: UnderLord7985
comments.body:
Sir iv only had a few bugs in the code im running that the AI is making, now i am very specific on what i want and how i want it done, knowing how to code is even better because then you can tell it exactly what to do and it understands that to a T. 

But if you are not specific enough it will go off the rails real quick, iv had a total of 15 bugs in a month of programmimg with the AI. Each one found by me and fixed by me using the AI, i told it exactly what the problem was and what i suspected caused the bug it goes in checks that out and if im wrong it'll let me know think iv had 2 bugs where i was wromg but the other 13 was spot on.
